edits.new: a 60 Mcps (million counts per second) count-rate ceiling and 0.1% afterpulsing [P]. Its passive recharge behaves paralyzably: a SPAD is live only if no photon arrived during the last dead time $\tau_d=6$ ns. A paralyzable counter counts at most $1/(e\tau_d)=1/(2.718\times6\ {\rm ns})=61$ Mcps, with $e$ Euler's number, which matches the measured 60 Mcps ceiling (§C5a, Eq. (76)); a non-paralyzable counter would instead approach $1/\tau_d=167$ Mcps. In the model's central "bright sun" case, half the background of a fully sunlit scene of reflectance 0.9 (the model's high case; §C0 subsection 10.3), each of the nine SPADs of a macro-pixel counts $r=3.66\times10^{8}/9=4.06\times10^{7}$ s⁻¹, so $r\tau_d=0.244$ and each SPAD is dead a fraction $1-e^{-0.244}=21.6\%$ of the time (Eq. - **Physics also bounds the minimum dwell:**
  - the round trip (1.67 µs at 250 m, $2\times250\ {\rm m}/c$);
  - scan-induced beam walk-off. During the round trip $2R/c$ the beam direction turns by $\Omega\cdot2R/c$, where $\Omega$ is the beam's angular scan rate (rad/s; for a spinning sensor, its rotation rate). At range $R$ the return therefore lands a lateral distance $\Delta x\approx2R^2\Omega/c$ away from where the receiver now looks. Waymo says this makes 360°, 10 Hz spinning "impractical for target ranges much above 100 m" and pushes designs to step-and-stare fast axes (point, dwell, then jump) [P].
- **The scan also bounds the maximum dwell:** a chirp that outlasts the beam's crossing time $\theta_b/\Omega$ (with $\theta_b\approx\lambda/D$ the beam's angular width and $D$ its diameter) is spread by scanner-induced Doppler (§C7, Eq. (86)). At a Falcon-class 45,600°/s (the polygon row of the §C7 table), even the 1.67 µs round trip to 250 m exceeds the crossing time of any beam wider than ≈1.2 mm unless the broadening is compensated digitally [E: the crossing time $\lambda/(D\Omega)$ falls below 1.67 µs for $D>\lambda/(\Omega\times1.67\ \mu{\rm s})=1.55\times10^{-6}/(796\times1.67\times10^{-6})=1.2$ mm].
edits.new:
- **Physics bounds the minimum dwell:** one round trip, $\tau=2R/c=2\times250\ {\rm m}/(3\times10^{8}\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}})=1.67$ µs at 250 m.
- **Walk-off bounds the scan rate.** During the round trip $2R/c$ the beam direction turns by $\dot\theta\cdot2R/c$, where $\dot\theta$ is the beam's optical scan rate (rad/s; for a spinning sensor, its rotation rate). At range $R$ the return therefore lands a lateral distance $\Delta x\approx2R^2\dot\theta/c$ away from where the receiver now looks. For a 360°, 10 Hz spin ($\dot\theta=2\pi\times10\ {\rm s^{-1}}=62.8$ rad/s) the lag angle $2R\dot\theta/c$ is $2\times100\ {\rm m}\times62.8\ {\rm s^{-1}}/(3\times10^{8}\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}})=4.2\times10^{-5}$ rad $=0.0024^\circ$ at 100 m and 0.006° at 250 m, against the 0.0036° 1/e² half-angle of a beam sized for 250 m (§C10.3a). Waymo says this makes 360°, 10 Hz spinning "impractical for target ranges much above 100 m" and pushes designs to step-and-stare fast axes (point, dwell, then jump) [P]; the lag angles above show why.
- **The scan also bounds the maximum dwell:** a chirp that outlasts the beam's crossing time $\theta_b/\dot\theta$ (with $\theta_b\approx\lambda/D$ the beam's angular width and $D$ its diameter) is spread by scanner-induced Doppler (§C7, Eq. (86)). At a Falcon-class 45,600°/s (the polygon row of the §C7 table), even the 1.67 µs round trip to 250 m exceeds the crossing time of any beam wider than ≈1.2 mm unless the broadening is compensated digitally [E: the crossing time $\lambda/(D\dot\theta)$ falls below 1.67 µs for $D>\lambda/(\dot\theta\times1.67\ \mu{\rm s})=1.55\times10^{-6}/(796\times1.67\times10^{-6})=1.2$ mm]. For any wider beam the minimum dwell already exceeds the maximum, so no chirp length works without digital compensation, as §C7b subsection 2(g) also finds for a 0.05° beam at 300 m.
edits.why: Walk-off bounds the scan rate, not the dwell; ties Waymo's 100 m claim to the lag numbers; states the min/max dwell conclusion.
